method: Read accessible source text; original page and paragraph or printed page is recorded. Source keys below are research keys, not Atlas S numbers. No claim is filled from memory. One short quotation per source, at most 25 words across its uses. Unread search snippets are explicitly distinguished.

sources.title: Triads, Coolies and Pimps: Chinatown in Former Times (NLB Biblio Asia, 2015)

sources.title: NAS, Lee Kuan Yew press conference, 9 August 1965, noon, pp.8,13 and19–22

sources.title: The Straits Times, 10 August 1965, p.1, Raja is named Foreign Minister (2015 facsimile reprint)
sources.read: Downloaded publisher’s facsimile and visually read lower-right contemporary article. Reports Monday 9 August reshuffle, lists all ten ministers and portfolios. Confirms Defence and Security, and Foreign Affairs and Culture. Later Culture transfer is outside this article.
sources.quote: Mr. Lee Kuan Yew today reshuffled his 10-man Cabinet

sources.title: Goh Lee Kim, The Making of the Causeway (NLB, 2024)
sources.read: Read full article, an edited extract of the jointly published Malaysian/Singapore National Archives book. Goods trains 17 September 1923, passenger trains 1 October 1923, official completion 11 June 1924, ceremony 28 June 1924.
sources.quote: The official opening of the Causeway on 28 June 1924

sources.title: Ang Seow Leng, Head Count: The History of Census-taking in Singapore (NLB, 2020)
sources.read: Full article, Early Censuses and Post-war Censuses; notes 5–16 and 41.
sources.quote: It was only on 2 April 1871 that the first systematic census of Singapore as part of the Straits Settlements was conducted.

sources.title: School Libraries Worldwide14(1), January2008, Table1,p.72 (indexed excerpt)
sources.read: Only indexed table text read. Its 1931 Others value appears as 8,275, unlike 8,295 in the original UN government return. This may be an OCR or printed error; original journal scan not independently inspected. It is kept as a conflicting lead rather than used to fill the census table.

sources.title: United Nations A/2134/Add.8, Singapore government return, 15 September 1952, printed p.2
sources.read: Downloaded the complete original government-return scan through the public ODS API. Visually read printed/PDF p.2; all six 1931 community groups and total confirmed. Others is 8,295, resolving the indexed secondary 8,275 discrepancy. Earlier research’s indexed page 6 label was corrected to printed p.2.
sources.quote: Singapore Island in recent decades has been as follows

sources.title: United Nations A/5079, Singapore, printed p.105
sources.read: Downloaded the complete 6.5 MB original UN government-return scan through the public ODS API. Visually read printed/PDF p.105; all six community groups and total confirmed. Footnote a/ marks the later estimate columns, not the 1957 census column. It excludes nonlocally domiciled Services personnel/families and transients afloat from those later estimates. The 1957 original census report remains unread.
sources.quote: non-locally domiciled Services personnel

sources.title: UK House of Commons, Detained Persons, 12 February 1963, vol.671, cols 171–172 W
sources.read: Complete primary parliamentary answer including names. Brockway 107 on 2 February; Sandys 110 on and since 2 February, about 100 that morning. Allegation of subversion remains government assertion.
sources.quote: 110 persons have been so detained on and since the 2nd February.

sources.title: Teo Chee Hean, Launch of The Battle for Merger reprint, 9 October 2014 (NAS transcript)
sources.read: Full 8 page primary government speech read, especially paragraphs 3–14, 19 and notes 4–6: official security interpretation and response to Thum.
sources.quote: there was a communist conspiracy to take power being played out over the merger issue

sources.title: Thum Ping Tjin, ARI Working Paper 211 (2013)
sources.read: Read pp.3–4, 16–21 and references there. Attributes political/anti-colonial interpretation; original British files not separately read. Paper mistakenly dates operation 3 February: primary Hansard supports 2 February.
sources.quote: their chief objections to merger were over the transfer of control of internal security laws

sources.title: Craven and Cate, The Army Air Forces in World War II, volume V, chapter 5, printed pp.155–162
sources.read: Team reading by the content agent; recorded in content-evidence-quotes.json. Read the original official USAAF history’s Singapore paragraphs on the 5 November 1944 dock attack, 11 January and 1 February 1945 dock attacks, 24 February Empire Dock attack and March oil-installation raids. It reports 53 aircraft attacking on 5 November and 39 percent of Empire Dock warehouse area destroyed on 24 February. These are attacker operational assessments; no verified civilian death total was found.
sources.quote: burn out 39 per cent of the warehouse area

sources.title: US Army Service Forces, Civil Affairs Handbook M354-18B: Japanese Administration of Occupied Areas, Malaya (25 August 1944), printed pp.2–3
sources.read: Team reading by the content agent; recorded in content-evidence-quotes.json. Read the indexed primary text of printed pp.2–3, Territorial Changes. It records the 20 August agreement and formal transfer of Perlis, Kedah, Kelantan and Trengganu on 18 October 1943, while Japanese forces retained strategic transport facilities. The full scan is too large for the browser and direct download returned HTTP 403; the source is not represented as fully read. US government work; no geometry derived.
sources.quote: The four states were formally transferred to Thailand on 18 October 1943

sources.title: Elections Department Singapore, 1959 Legislative Assembly General Election Results
sources.read: Team reading by the content agent, documented in content-extra-sources.json. Read all constituency tables. Recounted the highest Total Votes candidate in each table: 51 tables and 43 PAP winners. Reproducible tally in content-eld 1959-count.json; no number supplied from memory.

sources.title: Singapore Legislative Assembly, Order Paper No. 63, 5 September 1962, printed p. 153
sources.read: Team reading by the content agent, documented in content-extra-sources.json. Read both pages of the original order paper. The motion identifies 144,077 unmarked ballot papers and 2,370 uncertain ballot papers. It is an order paper proposing treatment of ballots, not evidence that the motion passed.

sources.title: Parliament of Singapore, Historical Development, sections1946–1965
sources.read: Team reading by the content agent, documented in content-extra-sources.json. Read institutional constitutional chronology: dissolution of Straits Settlements, separate Singapore colony, Penang/Malacca Malayan Union, limited 1948 elections, self-government and Malaysia. Dates and membership checked at the level of the institutional account; underlying Orders-in-Council not separately retrieved.

sources.title: NLB BiblioAsia, Time-honoured Temple Design (2016)
sources.read: Team reading by the content agent; recorded in content-evidence-quotes.json. Read historical foundation and successive rebuilding paragraphs: land allocated 1823, first wood-and-attap temple 1827, brick replacement 1843, major reconstruction 1862–63. This supports foundation chronology, not precise surveyed coordinates.
sources.quote: The temple that Pillai first built in 1827 was a simple wood-and-attap (palm frond) structure.

sources.title: Masjid Jamae (Chulia), official institutional history
sources.read: Team reading by the content agent; recorded in content-evidence-quotes.json. Read historical narrative and timeline on the mosque’s institutional website, including its 1826 origin and later building history. Location is South Bridge Road; no coordinate is asserted as newly surveyed.
sources.quote: An early wooden Masjid was established along South Bridge Road by the Tamil Muslim Chulia merchant community.

sources.title: NLB BiblioAsia, The Singapore Hokkien Huay Kuan Collection: A Treasure Trove of Information (2024)
sources.read: Team reading by the content agent; recorded in content-evidence-quotes.json. Read discussion of original land deeds and temple history: prayerhouse 1821, present temple construction  1839–1842, Telok Ayer Street shoreline. The deeds described by the article were not separately inspected.
sources.quote: began in 1839 and was completed by 1842

sources.title: NLB BiblioAsia, From Pauper to Philanthropist: The Tan Tock Seng Story (2017)
sources.read: Team reading by the content agent: NLB hospital funding and first-site paragraphs. Pearl’s Hill; foundation date 25 May 1844 conflicts with 25 July in the hospital’s own history and an NLB photograph catalog. Keep 1844 year precision; the exact original-site coordinate remains unverified.
sources.quote: On 25 May 1844, the foundation stone for the hospital

sources.title: Armenian Church Singapore, About the Armenian Church
sources.read: Team reading by the content agent: institutional account of 1835 construction and community links with India and Java. Consecration in 1836 is a separate date; precise coordinates were not verified.
sources.quote: the first Christian church built in Singapore in 1835

sources.title: NLB BiblioAsia, Land From Sand: Singapore’s Reclamation Story (2017)
sources.read: Team reading by the content agent: first reclamation, Collyer Quay and Telok Ayer paragraphs. The full scheme ran from 1879 to 1897, correcting the spec’s 1887 completion claim. Historical maps must establish each era’s shoreline; this prose does not supply a polygon.
sources.quote: Carried out between 1879 and 1897, it altered the shoreline of Telok Ayer

sources.title: Royal Malaysia Police, Pasukan Polis Negeri-Negeri Melayu Bersekutu
sources.read: Team reading by the content agent; recorded in content-evidence-quotes.json. Read full Malay institutional history; states federation became effective  1 July 1896  and lists four member states. A colonial agreement in 1895 and effective federation  1896 are distinct milestones.
sources.quote: pembentukan Negeri-Negeri Melayu Bersekutu yang berkuatkuasa pada 1 Julai 1896

sources.title: State of Perak, Dindings Cession (Amendment) Enactment 6 of 1954, Gazette 28 December 1954, p.901
sources.read: Team reading by the content agent; recorded in content-evidence-quotes.json. Read the complete indexed text of this one-page official enactment. Its preamble describes Dindings as ceded to Perak in 1935 and identifies the principal enactment as No.2/35. Direct scan retrieval timed out, so the precise handover day and principal enactment remain unverified; this source confirms the year only.
sources.quote: the territory of the Dindings, ceded to the State of Perak in 1935

sources.title: One Hundred Years of Singapore, volume I (1921), Historical chapter, p.31
sources.read: Team reading by the content agent; recorded in content-evidence-quotes.json. Read the public-domain OCR of printed p.31: Letters Patent dated 30 October 1906; incorporation in the Straits Settlements effective 1 January 1907; separate settlement from 1 December 1912. The original Letters Patent and proclamation were not independently retrieved. This contemporary colonial history is used for administrative chronology, not as a neutral account of colonial rule.
sources.quote: who duly proclaimed it as the ist January 1907

sources.title: Pangkor Engagement, 20 January 1874, reproduced by NUS Empire in Asia Documents Archive
sources.read: Team reading by the content agent; recorded in content-evidence-quotes.json. Read the full reproduced primary text, articles I–XIV and execution clause; the page identifies Allen, Stockwell and Wright, Collection of Treaties, volume I (1981), pp.390–392. Article VI requires Resident advice except Malay religion and custom; articles I–II concern the disputed succession. The prefatory colonial allegations are attributed rather than adopted as the topic’s narrative.
sources.quote: whose advice must be asked and acted upon on all questions other than those touching Malay Religion and Custom

sources.title: Jumaah Majlis DiRaja Johor, Kedaulatan dan Ketuanan Negeri Johor, section on the 11 December 1885 agreement
sources.read: Team reading by the content agent; recorded in content-evidence-quotes.json. Read the full Malay institutional account of the 1885 agreement and its seven clauses. It gives London, 11 December 1885, identifies the signatories and describes the consular agent and foreign-relations restrictions. Original treaty copies are pictured on the page but were not independently transcribed here. This is the Johor royal institution’s account; its evaluative claims are not reproduced.
sources.quote: Perjanjian Setia Kerajaan Johor-British 11 Disember 1885

sources.title: National Army Museum, Perak campaign medal, accession 2020-07-20-1-1
sources.read: Team reading by the content agent; recorded in content-evidence-quotes.json. Read the entire collection description. It dates the campaign 1875–1876, identifies British and imperial forces and Malay resistance, and links Birch’s killing to reinforcements and assaults on strongholds. It is a British military museum account, not a casualty register. No military or civilian total is inferred.
sources.quote: fought between British and imperial forces and Malay forces attempting to end foreign influence

sources.read: Read the complete official party history page in Malay. It dates the third Malay Congress/first UMNO general assembly and adoption of its constitution to 11 May 1946 at Istana Besar, Johor Bahru. This is the party’s institutional account, not the original 1946 constitution.
sources.quote: Pada 11 Mei 1946 di Istana Besar Johor Bahru.

sources.title: UK House of Lords, Brunei, 20 December 1962, vol. 245, cols. 1262–1266
sources.read: Read the complete contemporary statement and questions. Col. 1263 dates violence to 2 a.m. on 8 December and describes North Borneo police and British forces from Singapore. Its losses are provisional British government reports, not a final reconciliation.
sources.quote: the outbreak of violence at 2 a.m. on the morning of the 8th December

sources.title: UK House of Lords, Rising in Brunei, 10 December 1962, vol. 245, cols. 415–419
sources.read: Read the complete contemporary statement and questions. The minister identifies the North Kalimantan National Army, attacks on Brunei police/government buildings, the Sultan’s request for British help, British Army/Royal Marines/naval/air units and police from Sarawak/North Borneo. This is one government’s contemporaneous account; allegations about Azahari’s claims and plans must stay attributed.
sources.quote: an underground body which calls itself the North Kalimantan National Army

sources.title: National Archives of Singapore, All Must Vote, 1959 (9 September 2015)
sources.read: Read the full institutional article. It explicitly dates the first Cabinet’s swearing-in to 5 June 1959 and the election to 30 May. It is not the original appointment instrument or oath text.
sources.quote: The first cabinet of self-government was sworn in on 5 June 1959.

sources.title: NAS photograph B0033/30, Swearing-in of PAP Government at City Hall
sources.read: Read the complete original photograph catalog metadata: covering date 05/06/1959, negative B0033/30, Ministry of Information and the Arts Collection. Its description identifies Lee and Cabinet ministers after the ceremony. Catalog metadata corroborates the institutional date; the oath document itself was not read. Photo reproduction requires permission and is not proposed here.
sources.quote: SWEARING-IN OF PEOPLE'S ACTION PARTY (PAP) GOVERNMENT AT CITY HALL

sources.title: National Heritage Board, Kampong Glam Heritage Trail, printed pp. 4–5 and 38–39
sources.read: Downloaded the complete 4.96 MB official trail PDF. Read and visually inspected PDF pages 4 and 21 (printed pp. 4–5 and 38–39). The original mosque was constructed 1824–1826; the first timber Istana was completed in 1819, while Tunku Ali returned in 1840 and commissioned the current building. These are historical institutional summaries, not construction contracts.
sources.quote: the mosque was constructed between 1824 and 1826

sources.title: Official Penang State Courts portal, Sejarah Mahkamah Pulau Pinang
sources.read: Read the historical section in full, particularly its opening paragraph and the Butterworth section. It explicitly places British taking of Prince of Wales Island on 11 August 1786. This dates EIC possession, not the first human settlement of Penang. The original Francis Light journal was not read.
sources.quote: penaklukan Prince of Wales Island (Pulau Pinang) pada 11 Ogos 1786 oleh Kapten Francis Light

sources.title: Penang State Government, Sejarah, attributed to Lembaga Muzium Pulau Pinang
sources.read: Read the full Malay historical page. It dates British arrival to 1786 and explicitly records earlier habitation and Malay settlements. Used to prevent a British-possession date being presented as the origin of settlement.
sources.quote: Lama sebelum diambilalih oleh Syarikat Hindia Timur Inggeris kedua-dua kawasan ini telahpun mempunyai penghuni.

sources.title: Census of Population and Agriculture (Consolidation) Orders, O 1, Revised Edition 1990 (25 March 1992), table (a)
sources.read: Read the complete indexed legal order table returned by search, including the 1931 row (1 April 1931; G.N. 1956/30; 26 September 1930) and 1957 row. Direct page retrieval returned HTTP 403; do not claim a directly inspected original Gazette scan. A separate contemporary annual report’s reproduced text corroborates the distinction between reference night and enumeration.
sources.quote: 1st April 1931

sources.title: Straits Settlements Annual Report for 1931, Colonial Reports Annual no. 1599 (HMSO, 1932), printed p. 5; reproduced text
sources.read: Read the reproduced original report text, title/contents and printed pp. 1–6, especially the opening of Chapter III on p. 5. It states enumeration on 2 April 1931 as at midnight the previous night. This is directly read primary-report OCR/reproduced text on Scribd, not a downloaded or visually checked original scan. Do not transcribe its garbled community table. The official SSO indexed order independently states the reference night of 1 April.
sources.quote: A census of the population as at midnight on the previous night was taken on the 2nd April, 1931.

sources.title: Jason Heng, An Old Teochew Oral Account Sheds New Light on the 1819 Founding of Singapore (NLB, 2018)
sources.read: Read the complete article, especially the paragraph following the oral account, note 26 and settlement sections. It dates compelled relocation of the Temenggong’s Istana to Telok Blangah to 1823. Note 26 cites Buckley pp. 81–82, not an original relocation order read here. Year is confirmed at the institutional secondary level; an exact day remains unverified.
sources.quote: the British compelled the relocation of his* istana* (palace) to Telok Blangah in 1823

sources.title: Kwa Chong Guan, Remembering John Norman Miksic (NLB, 1 January 2026)
sources.read: Read the full institutional article. Its investigation paragraph dates the first Fort Canning dig from 18 to 28 January 1984 and reports pottery finds. This closes the 1984 start at institutional level; the 1985 original field report remains unread.
sources.quote: from 18 to 28 January 1984

sources.title: A Conspectus of the Labour Laws of Singapore, Malaya Law Review 10(2) (December 1968), p. 208, notes 35–36
sources.read: Read original scholarly PDF pp. 206–209, particularly p. 208 and notes 35–36. Distinguishes Indian Immigrants’ Protection Ordinance No. 1 of 1876, suspension in Singapore/Malacca under No. 5 of 1876 until 1883, and replacement No. 4 of 1884. It points to Gazette G.N. 577 of 28 December 1883. This resolves why several years coexist but does not substitute for reading the original ordinance and commencement notification.
sources.quote: not operative in Singapore until 1883

sources.title: Department of Museums Malaysia, Kota Johor Lama Historical Complex
sources.read: Directly read the complete institutional history, especially the first foundation paragraph. It dates Sultan Alauddin Riayat Shah II’s relocation to Tanjung Batu and construction of the fort to 1540. This confirms the year at museum-history level; it is not a directly inspected contemporary foundation instrument. Do not treat the fort date as the origin of all habitation along the river.
sources.quote: The history of Kota Johor Lama began in 1540

sources.title: Indonesian Ministry of Education and Culture, Decision 112/M/2018, Kawasan Cagar Budaya Pulau Penyengat, historical attachment pp. 10–11
sources.read: Downloaded the complete 113-page, 3.98 MB official decision copy. Visually inspected title/cover and PDF pages 11–13 (printed historical attachment pp. 9–11). Page 10 places Sultan Mahmud Syah III’s marriage to Engku Puteri Raja Hamidah and development of the island as government centre in 1803. Page 11 dates the shift from Hulu Riau to Daik to 1787. This is an original 2018 heritage instrument presenting historical findings, not original 1803/1787 documents. Its own text records an earlier defensive base in 1782–1784, so 1803 is not first habitation.
sources.quote: Pada tahun 1803 Sultan Mahmud Syah III menikah … ke Daik pada tahun 1787

sources.title: Portuguese Navy Cultural Directorate, Efeméride: Tomada de Malaca (24 August 2020)
sources.read: Read the full institutional museum article in Portuguese. Its heading and narrative identify the taking of Malacca on 24 August 1511, after Albuquerque sailed from India on 1 July. The same article describes the port’s importance before the Portuguese arrival. This confirms the conquest milestone at naval-museum level, not the foundation of Malacca and not an original 1511 instrument. Do not adopt its military numbers without independent scrutiny.
sources.quote: Tomada de Malaca, a 24 de Agosto de 1511

sources.title: British Military Administration, Malaya, Proclamation No. 1, signed 15 August 1945; reproduced in Singapore ICJ Memorial Annex 84, p. 743
sources.read: Downloaded the complete 13,084,375-byte, 221-page ICJ annex volume. Read OCR and visually inspected PDF page 143, Annex 84 p. 743: original Gazette reproduction of Proclamation No. 1, signed at Kandy on 15 August 1945, published in the Malay Peninsula Gazette no. 1 of 1 November 1945. Read all eight clauses. Clause 1 establishes BMA in areas of Malaya under forces’ control at any given time; clause 2 similarly conditions jurisdiction. Thus signing, publication, local military control and the 12 September surrender ceremony are distinct milestones. Do not infer Singapore control on 15 August.
sources.quote: Signed at Kandy, this 15th day of August, 1945. … under the control of Forces under my command

sources.title: Philip Jackson, Plan of the Town of Singapore (1822), original Commons/NAS scan
sources.read: Parent directly inspected the original 1846 × 1127 image and source-pixel traces; monochrome plan labels and street enclosures, no standalone colour legend.
sources.quote: European Town

facts.fact: 1896 Sarawak includes Limbang, acquired in 1890, and excludes Lawas, acquired in 1905. G 23 covers the Malay Peninsula and cannot establish Bornean boundaries.
Distinguish Australian command and BBCAU from Malayan BMA. British Borneo formally transferred to SEAC on 10 January 1946; exact local return of control dates remain unresolved.

Leyden pp. 40–43 tells the lion and naming story. Rockhill pp. 129–133 offers competing identifications for Lung-ya-men and Pan-tsu. Miksic 2013 chapter 4, Pires and the Nagarakretagama original passages were not read; precise modern locations remain unverified. The inspected Leyden passage has no Gregorian 1299; the origin of that later chronology was not established.

Gold discovery in 1928 confirmed; NLB reports ten ornaments, four surviving after the occupation. NHB indexed text supports Stone destruction in 1843 and an undeciphered inscription. Directly read NLB institutional history dates the first Fort Canning investigation to 18–28 January 1984. The original field report and complete assemblage remain unread.

NLB distinguishes ships off St John’s on 28 January from survey and landing variants on 29 January. Preliminary agreement: 30 January; treaty: 6 February. Buckley I pp. 35–42 records annual payments of 5,000 and 3,000 Spanish dollars. Exact landing spot and first person ashore remain disputed.

The spec’s approximately 1,000 total, 500 Orang Laut and 100–200 Malays could not be confirmed. NLB reports Marriott’s 150 including 30 Chinese, and Raffles’s 200; Saw p. 8 calls 150 an informed guess. These are estimates with differing geographical scopes, not a census. Do not force community estimates to add to a total.

Buckley I pp. 106–108 supports 7 June 1823 through contemporary correspondence. Allowances of 1,500 for the Sultan and 800 for the Temenggong were monthly. Pages 168–170: cession on 2 August 1824 covered the island and a ten geographical mile radius; lump sums 33,200/26,800 and monthly payments 1,300/700 respectively. The Anglo-Dutch original treaty was not independently inspected.

NAS supports formation in 1826, capital transfer in 1832 and Crown Colony status on 1 April 1867. The securely established date 27 November 1826 is the Second Charter of Justice; the exact administrative foundation day remains unverified.

First convicts in 1825 confirmed. NLB accounts disagree between 18 and 25 April. Ending transportation in 1860/1867 differs from the final convicts departing in May 1873. Do not call 1873 the transport abolition date. Annual totals remain unverified.

The Protectorate, Pickering and credit system abuses are confirmed for 1877; exact 1 May is unsupported by the read article. Low p. 3 records Chinese male arrivals of 195,613 in 1929,151,693 in 1930 and 49,723 in 1931. Earlier annual totals, mortality rates remain unverified. Indian immigration legislation is now distinguished as 1876 enactment, Singapore operation from 1883 and replacement in 1884 at secondary legal-history level; original instruments remain unread.

Kim gives a nineteenth century peak above 50% of Straits Settlements revenue, and 55% of total revenue in the early 1920s. Private farms continued until 1909. A uniform 40–50% claim and exact legal commencement of the 1910 monopoly/1946 ban still need original ordinances or Blue Books.

Buckley II p. 585 reports 400 or more deaths; NLB 2015 reports about 500. Both place onset on 5 May 1854 and duration at about ten days. Preserve both estimates. Exact end date 16 May remains unverified.

NLB 2020 gives 44 killed and more than 47 executed; the spec’s 47 killed is not confirmed. An indexed NHB teacher resource gives 47 executed. There were multiple executions; 25 March cannot stand for them all. Harper/Miller and Kuwajima originals were not read.

Copy ww 2 source text, IDs, dates, coordinates and routes unchanged. S 29’s 85,000 garrison includes 15,000 base and noncombatant personnel. Sook Ching spans 18 February–4 March; concentrated urban screening was 21–23 February (S 97). Changi: 66 on 20 February (S 98); Punggol: about 400 on 28 February (S 99). Keep attributed estimates separate.

11–13 December 1950; 18 deaths and 173 injured confirmed. NLB distinguishes attacks on civilians from police/military firing. A complete death count by community was not obtained. Seven people reported shot must not be silently treated as seven deaths.

12 May 1955: four dead and 31 injured. There were TWO police officers: Andrew Teo Bok Lan and Yuen Yau Pang; also student Chong Lon Chong and American journalist Gene Symonds. Who shot the student remains unresolved. The parade delay allegation is not an established finding.

NHB indexed text gives 13 dead and 123 injured; Poh’s participant account also reports 13 deaths. NLB confirms deregistration on 24 September, riots on 25–26 October and raids on 27 October. The spec’s exact 24–29 October interval and victim identities remain unverified.

The referendum on 1 September 1962 and rounded 71% for A / one quarter blank are confirmed. Percentages depend on the denominator: private raw totals imply 70.8% of all ballots. The content agent found a primary Order Paper giving 144,077 blank and 2,370 uncertain papers, differing from the private compilation’s 2,523 uncertain. Keep both, prioritise primary returns.

Primary Hansard, 12 February 1963: Brockway asks about 107 arrested on 2 February; Sandys answers 110 detained on and since that date, and about 100 that morning. Exact scopes for 113 and 111 remain unverified. Government security allegations and Poh/Thum’s political repression interpretation are attributed accounts.

UNTS volume 750, no. 10760 confirms the London agreement of 9 July 1963, its original 31 August date and the 28 August amendment to 16 September. Brunei was not a party. The precise causal chronology of the UN survey and the original Philippine claim documents remain unverified.

July: onset 21 July, 23 deaths and 454 injured. September: onset 2 September, 13 deaths and 106 injured; curfew ended 11 September and police stood down 14 September. The spec’s 3–7 September is corrected. The 12 death alternative remains unverified. July onset was near Kallang Road/Kampong Soo Poo; exact coordinates still need a source.

10 March 1965: three deaths and about 33 injured. Elizabeth (Suzie) Choo and Juliet Goh died immediately; Mohammed Yasin bin Kesit died later. The dedicated bombing article resolves the broader Federation article’s incomplete two death statement. The 1968 executions and Indonesian honours require separate attribution.

Trocki 1979 and Andaya 2017 passages were not obtained. Buckley’s colonial account alone cannot verify Engku Putri Hamidah’s exact role or adjudicate legitimacy. Borschberg’s original passage for destruction in 1613 was not read.

Malaysia Museums confirms Kota Johor Lama’s royal relocation/fort construction in 1540. Indonesia’s 2018 heritage decision, visually read historical pp. 10–11, dates Penyengat’s marriage gift/development as government centre to 1803 and the move of the royal government to Daik to 1787. These milestones are not first habitation. All proposed exact coordinates, the Stone position and competing Longyamen sites remain unverified.
NLB gives 1 February 1819; Buckley I p. 35 gives 5 February. Use early February in prose. Departure from Riau on 31 January remains unverified.
NLB dates Farquhar’s appointment to 6 February 1819; 7 February is Raffles’s departure.
NLB supports Penang departure on 19 January, Karimun rendezvous on 27 January and St John’s arrival on 28 January. Horsburgh describes the straits, but does not prove the 1819 ship’s precise track.
NHB’s original letter catalog places appointment in October 1822. The 4 November date belongs to Raffles’s instructions. Revise the beat’s appointment wording.
Foundation stone laid on 5 June 1823. Distinguish this ceremony from the later opening of the school.
The event says 7 June and the beat 9 June. Buckley I p. 108 supports 7 June.

G1 was directly inspected: it is monochrome sepia, with printed division names rather than a colour legend. Nine traced classes are recorded verbatim in jackson-legend.json; the two cantonments form one holder. Government-hill and Sultan-compound extents are interpreted street/plot enclosures, not observed ethnic residence. Historical junction continuity and allocation limits remain review gaps.

NHB indexed text connects Coleman Street to George D. Coleman. Crawford Street spelling and its Crawfurd connection still need direct evidence; Hill Street and Bencoolen Street etymologies were not directly verified.
27 November 1826 is the Second Charter date; the administrative formation day remains unverified. NAS supports the 1832 capital and 1 April 1867 Crown Colony dates.
An indexed Dutch proclamation dated 9 April 1825 was located in Leupe’s BKI reprint, but the original full passage was not read. Keep handover day provisional.
The precise reduction from three or four months to one month, forest clearance totals and tiger death figures were not verified. Do not supply numerical estimates.
Buckley I pp. 69–70 supports February 1821 for the first Amoy junk. Saw’s preview has 1812, apparently a typographical error; prefer the earlier account.

The 1968 legal article p. 208 and notes 35–36 distinguish Protection Ordinance No. 1 of 1876, its suspension in Singapore/Malacca until 1883, and replacement No. 4 of 1884. It points to Gazette G.N. 577 of 28 December 1883. Original legislation/commencement still unread. Protectorate establishment is supported in May 1877; exact 1 May remains unsupported.
Harris supports onset on 15 December 1876 and three killed by police fire. He contrasts the official secret society explanation with pressure on remittance and postal networks.
The precise Alexandra barracks and Outram Prison coordinates, 22 February endpoint and 25 March execution occasion were not located in original maps or records.

Low p. 3 supports male quotas from 1930, a falling male inflow, and exemption of women/children. January versus April commencement in 1933 remains unresolved. Samsui women came from Sanshui, Guangdong and worked in several occupations; avoid reducing their history to construction alone.
Individual resistance biographies were not independently read here; copy only existing ww 2 statements where available. Do not add unsupported details about Force 136, MPAJA or named civilians.

NLB places first arrivals in late December 1943, with about 3,000 inhabitants and about 500 deaths in 1944–45. The camp was five miles from Bahau town; the town coordinate does not establish the camp point.
1943 is supported by the Bahau account, but September, the official foundation on 14 December and a large group on 1 February 1944 have not been reconciled. Use year precision.

The Sultan Mosque reference is not proven riot onset. The incorrect Hock Lee point has been corrected to a qualified Dawson–Alexandra junction reference using the named official account, NHB trail text and georeferenced SLA OneMap tile. The depot gate and exact historical footprint remain unverified. See content-anchor-review.json, sources S260, S261 and S248.
Resignation on 7 June 1956 confirmed; the dispute concerned the proposed joint defence and internal security council’s veto arrangement.

Indexed UN Legislative Yearbook 1957 p. 287 gives Ordinance 35: assent 21 October, gazette 25 October and force from 1 November. NLB’s October wording is imprecise. The original commencement instrument remains unread.
Poh’s participant statement dates formation to 29 July 1961, correcting 26 July. Registration on 13 or 15 August remains unresolved.
NLB supports Subandrio’s policy announcement on 20 January 1963. An attack on 12 April would be a separate military event; that specific day was not independently verified.
NLB confirms Racial Harmony Day on 21 July since 1997 and goodwill committees. Exact initial committee membership and appointments were not independently checked.

Agreement dated 7 August 1965; Article II effective 9 August; NAS confirms 10 a.m. broadcast. Original Malaysian Hansard confirms 126 ayes, zero noes and ONE abstention in both readings. 22 December Act renamed the office President retrospectively from 9 August. Contemporary Lee and Razak statements, Malaysian diplomatic reporting and Goh’s notes give attributed accounts; the two memoirs were not directly read.

The read NLB extract of the joint National Archives book confirms the official opening on 28 June 1924. Distinguish goods trains 17 September 1923, passenger trains 1 October 1923 and official completion 11 June 1924.

Primary Hansard 9 May 1927 quotes the inquest jury: six men died from police gunshots outside Kreta Ayer Police Station. Exact 12 Marchday still needs the original dated account; month precision is secure. The inquest and official description remain attributed.

The Straits Times 10 August 1965 p 1 contemporary article reports Monday 9 August’s reshuffle and all ten ministers. Goh: Defence and Security; Rajaratnam: Foreign Affairs and Culture; Lim: Finance; Barker: Law and National Development; other portfolios retained. NAS noon transcript independently confirms Goh’s title. A later Culture transfer date remains unverified.
The spec’s P 34 reference to “Lim & Lau” does not identify the Lim author or title. Do not infer a book. Albert Lau’s listed work remains a bibliographic lead unless the passage was actually read.

1824: 10,683. The 1871 census was on 2 April: 97,111 in Marriott; Saw 2007 gives 96,087, scope unresolved. Read government scans confirm 1931 total 557,745 and 1957 UN return 1,445,929, including six community groups. SIT 1959 instead reports 1,445,930 with small group differences. Both are retained; the later UN footnote expressly qualifies estimate columns, so no census-scope inference is silently added.

Nine Cabinet names and portfolios are confirmed in ISEAS finding aid DM.070.003. The content agent counted 43 PAP winners in ELD’s 51 results; direct ELD chronology confirms electorate 586,098 and compulsory voting. NAS institutional history plus photograph catalog B0033/30 confirm swearing-in on 5 June 1959. The original appointment instrument remains unread.

Team readings confirm Sri Mariamman 1827, Jamae 1826, Thian Hock Keng 1839–1842 and Armenian Church 1835 (consecration 1836). TTSH’s 1844 foundation day conflicts: NLB 25 May versus hospital/NLB catalog 25 July; use year only. NLB dates the full Telok Ayer scheme 1879–1897 rather than 1887; an 1887 map can still represent an intermediate coast. NHB’s trail scan confirms original Sultan Mosque construction 1824–1826. Precise coordinates and St Andrew’s details remain unchecked here.

Team readings support Pangkor 20 January 1874 (full treaty text), FMS effective 1 July 1896, Johor treaty 11 December 1885 (royal institutional account), Labuan incorporation 1 January 1907 (contemporary published history) and Perak campaign 1875–1876. A Perak 1954 enactment confirms Dindings cession in 1935, but 16 February remains unverified. Johor’s 1914 adviser date still needs its instrument. Treaty 1909 signing 10 March versus ratification 9 July remains distinct.

Team reading of the indexed US Army 1944 handbook confirms formal transfer of the four states on 18 October 1943 while Japan retained strategic transport facilities; the full scan was not obtained. The official USAAF history was read for 5 November 1944–March 1945 raids. Its aircraft and warehouse figures are attacker operational assessments; civilian casualties remain unverified.

Direct ELD institutional chronology confirms six elected seats in 1948 and registered electorate 22,395, rising to 300,299 in 1955 after automatic registration from 1954. The exact 20 March 1948 and 2 April 1955 days were not independently verified from an original election writ here; team institutional chronology provides context.

ELD confirms automatic registration from 1954, electorate 300,299 in 1955 and 586,098 in 1959. Its published 1959 turnout percentage conflicts with its raw counts, so omit that percentage. The first official use of flag/arms/anthem and Yusof’s 3 December oath still need original instruments or recordings.

Direct ELD chronology confirms election on 21 September 1963. Contemporary Hansard confirms the Brunei outbreak on 8 December and identifies opposing forces as the British government account. The exact constitutional meaning of Lee’s 31 August declaration remains unchecked here.

The original Order in Council SI 1948/108, section 3, explicitly makes the Order and State/Federation Agreements operative on 1 February 1948. The agreement itself, reproduced in the Second Schedule, is dated 21 January. Singapore was outside the Federation.
UMNO’s complete official history dates formal founding through adoption of its constitution to 11 May 1946 at Istana Besar, Johor Bahru.

NAS institutional history and photo B0033/30 metadata independently place the first Cabinet swearing-in at City Hall on 5 June 1959. This closes the ceremony day; appointment instrument and oath text remain unread.

Contemporary Hansard explicitly dates the outbreak to 2 a.m. on 8 December 1962. The British minister names TNKU, Brunei police, British Army/Royal Marines/naval/air forces and police reinforcements from Sarawak/North Borneo. The Sultan requested aid. These are British government accounts; rebel objectives and alleged plans remain attributed until their own documents are read.

NHB trail printed pp. 4–5 and 38–39, visually inspected: first timber Istana completed in 1819; present building commissioned after Tunku Ali returned in 1840; original Sultan Mosque constructed in 1824–1826. These are different structures, with no exact construction day asserted.

Penang Courts dates British taking of Prince of Wales Island to 11 August 1786. The state museum account confirms earlier Malay habitation and settlements, so use EIC possession or British settlement as the event rather than first settlement.
Directly read NLB account dates the Temenggong’s compelled relocation to Telok Blangah to 1823. Exact day and original relocation order remain unread.

The SSO consolidated order’s indexed table gives the night of 1 April 1931 (G.N. 1956/30, notified 26 September 1930). The contemporary 1931 annual report, directly read as reproduced text, says the census was taken on 2 April as at midnight the previous night. Reference date and enumeration day are distinct. Neither the SSO original Gazette nor this annual-report scan was inspected visually.

The Portuguese Navy’s full museum account dates the capture of Malacca to 24 August 1511 and describes its earlier trading-port history. Use this as a political-control milestone, not settlement foundation. No original 1511 account or precise site coordinate was inspected.

The original Proclamation No. 1 was signed at Kandy on 15 August 1945. Clause 1 applies BMA to areas of Malaya under forces’ control at a given time; Singapore is within the named geographical scope, but this is not proof of control there on the signing day. The original reproduced Gazette is dated 1 November. Retain 12 September only as the surrender-ceremony milestone; local assumption of control needs separate evidence.
